rationale: B wins because it turns the same facts into four cleaner, more separable stories. Its "Rivian's new stalls will speak both plugs — CCS and NACS on every one" finds a real infrastructure-design angle that A mostly leaves on the floor, while A spends a slot on "Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network," which is shiny but under-proved by the update. A is useful, but B is the one I would trust not to walk a founder into Tesla-bait before the evidence is there.
gaps_in_A: "Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" overstates the competitive frame. The update says NACS plugs and open access; it does not say Rivian is positioning against Tesla.
"following the industry's shift away from automaker-exclusive plugs" imports a broad trend that needs outside sourcing. A admits that later, but the headline-level frame still leans on it.
The first and fourth angles both orbit brand-agnostic charging-network strategy. The set would be stronger if one slot isolated the CCS/NACS infrastructure-design story instead.

"Rivian CEO explains the strategy behind opening the network" is rightly refused for lack of a named exec, but A misses a valid version: an on-record company strategy interview could work if secured after the proof is gathered.
gaps_in_B: "The prevailing belief: a proprietary fast-charging network is a moat" is a smart premise, but it is not in the supplied update. It needs an analyst, prior coverage, or company comment before it becomes load-bearing.
"Every other EV driver just gained 3,500 fast chargers" is a little too sweeping until compatibility, geography, and access mechanics are nailed down. Service journalism dies on those details.
"journalist-fit-check" is slightly premature as the next step. Pick the proof-backed angle and build a targeted list first; fit-check comes once real names are on the table.
